result: Magnesium increases antibiotic resistance in Vibrio species and other bacteria. The authors demonstrate that high magnesium concentrations (50-200 mM MgCl2) dramatically increase MICs for balofloxacin (BLFX) and other antibiotics (quinolones, β-lactams, aminoglycosides, etc.) in V. alginolyticus, V. parahaemolyticus, and carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'produced convincing evidence indicating that in high concentrations of magnesium, the efficacy of selected antibiotics was diminished.' Reviewers 2 and 3 both note the authors 'succeeded in their goals' and used 'a variety of methodologies, all of which point to a clear effect of exogenous Mg2+ on drug resistance.' No concerns were raised about these fundamental MIC measurements.

result: Magnesium modulates fatty acid biosynthesis by increasing saturated fatty acids (palmitic acid, stearic acid) and decreasing unsaturated fatty acids (palmitoleic acid, linoleic acid, linolenic acid, stearidonic acid). This was demonstrated through GC-MS and LC-MS metabolomics showing dose-dependent changes in fatty acid profiles.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these metabolomic findings. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors have shown the significance of fatty acid biosynthesis pathway behind the resistance mechanism' and notes the study demonstrates 'the role of an exogenous factor in altering membrane composition.' Reviewer 3 commends 'a comprehensive study, spanning evaluation of whole cell phenotypes, metabolic pathways, genetic manipulation, to enzyme activity level evaluation.' No concerns were raised about the metabolomics data or fatty acid measurements.

result: Exogenous fatty acids modulate antibiotic susceptibility: unsaturated fatty acids (linolenic acid) increase bacterial susceptibility to BLFX while saturated fatty acids (palmitic acid) decrease susceptibility. The two fatty acid types antagonize each other in the presence of BLFX, and magnesium has minimal effect on this antagonism.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these functional validation experiments. Reviewer 1 notes the study showed 'decreased biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids and PE, along with an increase in the biosynthesis of PG' led to reduced antibiotic efficacy. Reviewer 2 states 'additional experiments were performed as suggested by the reviewers which certainly enhanced the quality of the paper,' suggesting these fatty acid supplementation experiments were part of revisions that satisfied reviewer concerns. No specific critiques of these experiments were raised.

result: Magnesium remodels glycerophospholipid metabolism by reducing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) biosynthesis and increasing phosphatidylglycerol (PG) production. Lipidomics data showed PE levels declined while PG levels increased with increasing Mg2+, along with changes in specific lipid species.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these lipidomics findings. Reviewer 1 states the study 'produced convincing evidence' for 'decreased biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids and PE, along with an increase in the biosynthesis of PG.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the fact that the authors uncovered a molecular mechanism underlying Mg2+-induced phenotypic resistance is particularly important as the key proteins should be studied further,' indicating acceptance of the phospholipid metabolism findings. No concerns were raised about the lipidomics data.

result: Magnesium-induced membrane changes decrease membrane permeability, fluidity, and increase polarization, thereby reducing antibiotic uptake. This was demonstrated through fluorescence assays (DiBAC4(3), FM5-95, SYTO9) and LC-MS measurements of intracellular BLFX levels.
evaluation: Reviewers support these membrane biophysics findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the study 'sheds light on the role of an exogenous factor in altering membrane composition, polarization and fluidity which ultimately leads to antimicrobial resistance.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors used 'a variety of methodologies, all of which point to a clear effect' and commends the comprehensive approach. No specific concerns were raised about the membrane permeability or fluidity measurements.

result: Magnesium regulates fatty acid metabolism through transcriptional regulators (FadR, ArcA, FabR) and key enzymes (FabA, FabF, FadL). Gene expression and protein abundance data showed magnesium increases expression of fatty acid biosynthesis genes while decreasing degradation genes. Deletion mutants (ΔfadR, ΔarcA) showed reduced viability with BLFX.
evaluation: Reviewers support these molecular mechanism findings. Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'the fact that the authors uncovered a molecular mechanism underlying Mg2+-induced phenotypic resistance is particularly important as the key proteins should be studied further,' indicating acceptance of the genetic and protein-level data. Reviewer 2 states 'additional experiments were performed as suggested by the reviewers which certainly enhanced the quality of the paper,' suggesting these genetic experiments may have been part of satisfactory revisions. No specific concerns were raised about the qRT-PCR, Western blot, or mutant data.

result: Magnesium modulates phospholipid biosynthesis enzymes: PGS levels increase while PSS levels decrease with increasing Mg2+. Enzyme activity assays confirmed Mg2+ reduces PSS activity. Deletion mutants (ΔplsB, ΔpgpA) showed reduced viability with BLFX.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these enzyme activity and genetic findings as part of the overall molecular mechanism. Reviewer 3 commends the study for 'spanning evaluation of whole cell phenotypes, metabolic pathways, genetic manipulation, to enzyme activity level evaluation,' indicating acceptance of the enzyme activity data. No specific concerns were raised about the ELISA measurements or enzyme activity assays.

result: Mechanistic interpretations and inferences: PE may inhibit and PG may promote BLFX resistance; the ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids may predict antibiotic resistance; magnesium functions through lipid metabolism; glycolysis fluxes into fatty acid biosynthesis under high magnesium; membrane depolarization may influence resistance.
evaluation: While reviewers generally accept the data, Reviewer 3 notes 'the conclusions drawn by the authors are justified by the data, except for the interpretation of some experiments,' suggesting some mechanistic interpretations may be overreaching. These claims are largely inferential or speculative rather than directly demonstrated, and the reviewer's caveat indicates some uncertainty about interpretations despite accepting the underlying data.
